content: Recurrent miscarriage affects approximately 1% to 3% of women of reproductive age, with most cases occurring before the 10th week of gestation. These miscarriages often recur around the same gestational week in subsequent pregnancies. While some cases of recurrent miscarriage can be attributed to identifiable causes related to the mother or fetus, many cases remain unexplained, with no underlying cause identified. For unexplained recurrent miscarriage, there is currently no universally accepted treatment. Chinese herbal medicines have been used for thousands of years in Asian societies and have recently gained popularity as an alternative to Western medicine. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of Chinese herbal medicines in treating unexplained recurrent miscarriage. To conduct this review, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, Embase, CINAHL, and several Chinese databases, up to June 1, 2015. They also reviewed reference lists of relevant studies and contacted experts and manufacturers in the field. The inclusion criteria were randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing Chinese herbal medicines (alone or in combination with other treatments) to placebo, no treatment, other interventions (e.g., bed rest or psychological support), or Western pharmaceuticals. Cross-over studies were excluded. Nine randomized clinical trials involving 861 women were included in the review. These trials compared Chinese herbal medicines, either alone or in combination with Western pharmaceuticals, to Western pharmaceuticals alone. One study compared Chinese herbal medicines combined with psychotherapy to psychotherapy alone. No trials compared Chinese herbal medicines to placebo or no treatment. The formulations of Chinese herbal medicines varied across the trials, with some using modified classical formulations. The Western pharmaceuticals used in the studies included tocolytic drugs (e.g., salbutamol, magnesium sulfate), hormonal supplements (e.g., human chorionic gonadotropin, progesterone, dydrogesterone), and supportive supplements (e.g., vitamin E, vitamin K, folic acid). The methodological quality of the included studies was generally poor, with an unclear risk of bias in most domains. When comparing Chinese herbal medicines alone to Western pharmaceuticals alone, there was no significant difference in the live birth rate (risk ratio [RR] 1.05; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.67 to 1.65; one trial, 80 women). Data on pregnancy continuation beyond 20 weeks were not available for this comparison. However, when Chinese herbal medicines were combined with Western pharmaceuticals, the continuing pregnancy rate (RR 1.27; 95% CI 1.10 to 1.48; two trials, 189 women) and live birth rate (average RR 1.55; 95% CI 1.14 to 2.10; six trials, 601 women) were higher compared to Western pharmaceuticals alone. For the comparison of Chinese herbal medicines combined with psychotherapy versus psychotherapy alone, the live birth rate was also higher in the combination group (RR 1.32; 95% CI 1.07 to 1.64; one trial, 90 women). Data on pregnancy continuation beyond 20 weeks were not available for this comparison. Adverse effects and toxicity rates for the mother and fetus were not reported in most studies. Two trials (341 women) reported no maternal adverse effects, and one trial reported no abnormal fetal outcomes based on ultrasound or post-delivery assessments. No data were available for the review's secondary outcomes. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence to assess the effectiveness of Chinese herbal medicines for unexplained recurrent miscarriage due to the small sample sizes and poor methodological quality of the included studies. While a combination of Chinese herbal medicines and Western pharmaceuticals may improve continuing pregnancy and live birth rates compared to Western pharmaceuticals alone, the safety of these interventions for the mother and baby remains unclear. No trials compared Chinese herbal medicines alone to placebo or no treatment. The authors emphasized the need for high-quality studies to further evaluate the effectiveness and safety of Chinese herbal medicines for unexplained recurrent miscarriage. Future research should include placebo-controlled trials, proper randomization methods, and assessments of safety outcomes, such as maternal and perinatal adverse effects and toxicity. Addressing these methodological issues would provide more reliable evidence on the role of Chinese herbal medicines in managing unexplained recurrent miscarriage.
